inline.s: Master Xing'an's Commentary on the Western Rebirth Vow says: "'The faculties' refers to the five faculties such as the eye; 'right mindfulness' is the faculty of mind. Free of illness and hindrance, therefore serene and joyful; free of greed and delusion, therefore clear and distinct. Relinquishing the body one has received is called relinquishing the reward-body; unhurried and unruffled, therefore peaceful and dignified; passing away seated or standing in death, therefore it is said to be like entering Chan samādhi."

[At that time I, riding upon the diamond dais, following behind the Buddha, within the interval of a finger-snap, was born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, within a superior lotus blossom in the pool of seven treasures. When the blossom opened, I saw the Buddha, beheld all the Bodhisattvas, heard the wondrous sound of Dharma, and attained the patience of non-arising.]

At that time, riding upon the diamond dais and following behind the Buddha, within the snapping of a finger I was born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, within a superior lotus blossom in the pool of seven treasures. The lotus at once opened, and I saw Amitābha Buddha and all the great Bodhisattvas, heard the subtle and wondrous sound of Dharma, and upon hearing, realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.

[Diamond dais] This is the throne of one born in the highest grade. The Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life says: When one born in the highest grade is reborn in that land (the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss), "because this person is vigorous and brave, Amitābha Tathāgata, together with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, countless transformation Buddhas, hundreds and thousands of monks and the great assemblies of śrāvakas, immeasurable devas, and palaces of seven treasures — with Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva holding the diamond dais and, together with Mahāsthāmaprāpta, coming before the practitioner — Amitābha Buddha releases a great radiant light, illumining the practitioner's body, and, with all the Bodhisattvas, extends a hand in welcome." [Within a finger-snap] describes an extremely brief time: within a finger-snap.

[Superior lotus blossom] the lotus (flower) within which there is the diamond dais. [Patience of non-arising] that is the patience of non-arising dharmas, in which true wisdom abides in the principle that "all dharmas originally never arose, and so also never cease," and never again falls back. The Buddha says: "All dharmas are all false and unreal." (Great Parinirvāṇa Sutra, Volume Forty

the Kaundinya Chapter.) All dharmas originally neither arise, and so also do not cease. Yet sentient beings invert true and false, falsely seeing arising and ceasing. Now upon hearing the subtle, wondrous sound of Dharma, one at once opens wisdom and understands that dharmas originally have no arising or ceasing — hence it is said one "attains the patience of non-arising." Having obtained the patience of non-arising, one is a great being of the Dharma-body, endowed with vast spiritual powers and wondrous functions.

[Within a moment, I attended upon all the Buddhas and personally received the prophecy. Having received the prophecy, the three bodies, the four wisdoms, the five eyes, the six supernormal powers, the immeasurable hundreds and thousands of dhāraṇī gates, and all meritorious virtues were completely accomplished.]

Within a moment I attended upon and made offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, and personally received the prophecy of the Buddhas. Having received the prophecy of Buddhahood, the three bodies (the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, the Response-body), the four wisdoms (the wisdom of accomplishing works, the wisdom of wondrous observation, the wisdom of equality, and the wisdom of the great perfect mirror), the five eyes (the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye), the six supernormal powers (the divine eye, the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the recollection of past lives, the power of spiritual transformation, and the extinction of defilements), the immeasurable hundreds and thousands of dhāraṇī (retention) gates, and all meritorious virtues — all completely accomplished.

[A moment] an instant. [Bestowal of the prophecy] The Buddha, in advance, names the Bodhisattva: after so many eons, at a certain place in a certain land, what Buddha he will become. [Three bodies] the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Response-body. Using the moon, its light, and its reflection as a simile: the Dharma-body is like the moon, the Reward-body like the light, and the Response-body like the reflection. [Four wisdoms] the wisdom of accomplishing works, the wisdom of wondrous observation, the wisdom of equality, and the wisdom of the great perfect mirror. The "wisdom of accomplishing works" is accomplished by transforming the five defiled consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousness) and is the wisdom by which a Buddha succeeds in accomplishing all deeds that benefit all sentient beings. The "wisdom of wondrous observation" is accomplished by transforming the defiled sixth consciousness (the ideating consciousness) and is the wisdom by which a Buddha observes all dharmas and the capacities of all sentient beings, administering medicine according to the ailment and turning the ordinary into the sage. The "wisdom of equality" is accomplished by transforming the defiled seventh consciousness (the manas) and is the wisdom by which a Buddha penetrates the principle of nonself and equality and, toward all sentient beings, gives rise to unconditional great compassion. The "wisdom of the great perfect mirror" is accomplished by transforming the defiled eighth consciousness (ālaya) and is the wisdom by which a Buddha contemplates all phenomenal marks and noumenal principle, none of it being unclear; this wisdom is pure and perfectly luminous, seeing clearly both within and without, like a great perfect mirror clearly illumining all things. [Five eyes] the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye. The fleshly eye is the eye of ordinary beings in a physical body; encountering darkness or obstruction, it cannot see. The divine eye is the eye of devas, able to see near and far, day and night. The wisdom eye is the eye of the śrāvaka, able to see through false appearances and recognize true emptiness. The Dharma eye is the eye of the Bodhisattva, able to clearly comprehend all the Dharma-gates of the worldly and the transmundane. The Buddha eye is the eye of the Tathāgata; with the Buddha eye one also possesses the preceding four eyes, able to know all things and see all things; among all dharmas, the Buddha eye constantly shines. [Dhāraṇī gate] the method of total retention. The Sanskrit "dhāraṇī" means "total retention," because it retains the good so that it does not scatter and restrains the evil so that it does not arise. For example, the Bodhisattva, through the method of total retention, adapts to the speech of all sentient beings, guiding them to right faith, causing them to extinguish all evil thoughts and to practice all good dharmas — this is the Bodhisattva's dhāraṇī gate.

At this time, returning into the Saha world to universally save sentient beings, so as to fulfill the vow to save the four kinds of kindness, the three realms, and the sentient beings of the Dharma-realm.

[Then, without departing from the Land of Peace and Nurture, I return into the Saha world. Manifesting countless bodies, filling the lands of the ten directions; with inconceivable, sovereign spiritual power and every kind of skillful means, I deliver sentient beings, causing them all to leave defilement and regain a pure mind, to be born together in the West, and to enter the ground of non-retrogression.]

Then, without the self-nature departing from the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, transformation bodies appear in the Saha world, manifesting countless bodies — like one moon reflected in a thousand rivers — filling the lands of the ten directions. With inconceivable, sovereign spiritual power and every kind of skillful means, I deliver sentient beings, causing them all to leave defilement and recover the pure mind of the self-nature, to be born together in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and to enter the stage of non-retrogression.

[Without departing from the Land of Peace and Nurture] the self-nature does not depart from the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. "Land of Peace and Nurture" is another name for the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life says: "The Buddhas tell the Bodhisattvas to go visit the Buddha of the Land of Peace and Nurture." [Ground of non-retrogression] the stage of non-retrogression, transliterated "Avivartika." This means that having been born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss one only advances to Buddhahood and never regresses. [Land] transliterated "kṣetra," translated as "field," "land," "country," "place" — that is, the land of a Buddha; combining Sanskrit and Chinese, "buddha-field." "Buddha-field" means the land of a Buddha.
Summing up the great vows set forth above.
[Such great vows — as long as the worlds are inexhaustible, sentient beings inexhaustible, karma and all the afflictions inexhaustible, my vows are inexhaustible.]
The above are the great vows I have made: as long as the worlds are without end, sentient beings without end, karma and afflictions without end, so too my great vows have no time of ending.
The vow text having come to this point, whether self or other, cause or effect, phenomenal or noumenal, it is all perfect and ultimate; therefore it ends with a dedication of merit.

[Dedication] the merit one has cultivated, not wishing to enjoy it alone, one turns it back and directs it to the sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, sharing it with them, so as to broaden one's own mind and so that the merit has a clear direction without being dissipated.

[May the merit of now bowing to the Buddha, making these vows, and cultivating be turned and given to living beings. May the four kinds of kindness be all requited and the three realms be universally aided. May the sentient beings of the Dharma-realm together perfect the wisdom of all modes.]

May these various merits of bowing to the Buddha, making vows, and cultivating be turned and bestowed upon sentient beings, universally requiting the four deep kindnesses, and delivering, without distinction, all beings of the three realms from suffering. May all beings in the Dharma-realm together perfect the wisdom of the Buddha.

[Wisdom of all modes] an abbreviation of the wisdom of all modes, that is, the wisdom of the Buddha. This wisdom can know the single mark of all dharmas and can also know that the many marks are nondual and non-different, and is therefore called the wisdom of all modes.
Master Xing'an's Commentary on the Western Pure Land Text says:

In Bodhisattva practice one must first dedicate the merit, for if one does not dedicate, the retribution is that of humans and devas; if one can dedicate, then it becomes the right cause of transcending the world. There are three dedications: first, dedicating self to others; second, dedicating the cause to the fruit; third, dedicating the phenomenal to the noumenal. What is "dedicating self to others"? Because since beginningless time the wholesome karma one has cultivated has all been for one's own body and one's own kin; now one turns this mind toward sentient beings, giving them all that one has cultivated, wishing them to gain benefit and not seeking one's own joy — this is called "dedicating self to others." What is "dedicating the cause to the fruit"? Because since beginningless time one has sought only the blessings of humans and devas and not the real fruit that transcends the world; now one turns this mind toward the supreme bodhi, using all the wholesome karma one has cultivated to adorn the Buddha-fruit — this is called "dedicating the cause to the fruit." What is "dedicating the phenomenal to the noumenal"? If one sees sentient beings, Buddhas, and wholesome dharmas as having a variety of distinctions in the dedication, then the phenomenal is not empty. Now one turns this mind toward the reality-limit; the one who can cultivate and what is cultivated, the one who can dedicate and what is dedicated — both are extinguished — this is called "dedicating the phenomenal to the noumenal." Here "the kindness and the three realms are all aided" is "dedicating self to others"; "together perfecting the wisdom of all modes" is "dedicating the cause to the fruit." These two are both phenomenal marks, and the noumenal lies within the phenomenal, so all three are complete. "Wisdom of all modes" is the wisdom of the Buddha, meaning able to know the single mark of dharmas and also to know the many marks as nondual and non-different, and is therefore called this.

Question: The wholesome karma one cultivates, though it exists and as if it does not, is called not dwelling in marks. Now as soon as a single deed is finished, one is eager to dedicate — is this not attachment? Answer: You say good karma does not dwell in marks; does it have future retribution or not? If not, then one falls into annihilation; if yes, then though one does not seek blessings, blessings still follow one — the retributions of humans and devas can hardly be left behind. How is that non-attachment? Now by turning this merit to sentient beings and to the Buddhas, it becomes an undefiled, supreme cause — what attachment is there? Question: When the merit is turned to sentient beings, do they actually gain benefit? If no benefit, then it is vain and false; if benefit, then I act and others receive — how can this be? Answer: The Bodhisattva's merit is shared together with sentient beings. Though at present there is no benefit, in the future when he becomes a Buddha, sentient beings receive its gift. As in the Buddha-land of Amitābha: whoever is born there enjoys the same as the Buddha; and it is because the World-Honored One, in his causal stage, made merit and turned it to us that today we obtain its retribution — like a father's wealth used by the son, who can say it is not right? Question: Between dedicating and not dedicating, is there a superiority or inferiority in the merit, and a gain or loss in the deed? Answer: With dedication little merit becomes much, like a drop cast into the sea, impossible to distinguish; without dedication much merit turns to little, like pouring water into a leaking goblet (the "goblet"
zhī

, a vessel of the ancients for holding wine), which in a moment is empty. Moreover, if one can dedicate, then the mind can turn the merit and go straight to the West; if one does not dedicate, then the mind is pulled along by the merit and again born in the three realms. Therefore one who cultivates the Pure Land, having even a single good deed, first dedicates it to the West — precisely because of this. Question: To dedicate to the West is to seek one's own happiness, and to dedicate to the Buddha-fruit is to seek one's own honor and supremacy; from of old it is for oneself — what does it have to do with sentient beings? Answer: If one were not for others, why would one need to become a Buddha? If not for bringing order to disorder, what use to seek kingship? You should know that benefiting others must begin with benefiting oneself, and perfecting oneself is perfecting others — how can there still be a division of self and other? Question: Sentient beings are originally empty, bodhi is nonexistent, and wholesome dharmas are not seen — what is there to dedicate? Answer: Though one knows these three are all empty, sentient beings do not understand, and falsely create all karma and falsely undergo all suffering. Therefore the Bodhisattva dedicates wholesome dharmas for them, and moreover, wishing to become a Buddha to deliver them, does not abandon the cultivation of cause and effect. But if one grasps at the all-emptiness, one instead falls into a one-sided view, dropping into the deep pit of the two vehicles' annihilation. Hence one must know that being complete in the three dedications is the essential practice of the Bodhisattva's cultivation, and one must not be without this knowledge."
[Note] Readers who understand the first (ultimate) meaning may further read the Explanation of the Western Rebirth Vow below.

blocks.text: Introduction to the Explanation of the Western Rebirth Vow

inline.s: Annotated by Zhanran

In the verse, the first two lines are taking refuge in the great guide Amitābha Buddha, who welcomes and leads sentient beings to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; the last two lines are making the vow to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, praying for the compassionate protection of Amitābha Buddha.

blocks.text: 2. Repenting and Removing the Three Hindrances

inline.s: This is the four great vows. If a cultivator has no vows, then there is retrogression; therefore with these four one restrains one's own mind, and so does not give rise to indolence. These four great vows, resting upon the non-doing four noble truths of the perfect teaching, are called profound vows. If the vow does not rely on the truths, it is called a mad vow. If it is not non-doing, it is likewise not called profound. As for "non-doing," it means that the nature is originally complete and all four are without any contrivance. The Tiantai Master says: By delusion regarding the principle, nirvāṇa is taken as birth and death, and this is called the truth of suffering; bodhi is taken as affliction, and this is called the truth of accumulation. By awakening to the principle, birth and death are realized as nirvāṇa, and this is called the truth of cessation; affliction is realized as bodhi, and this is called the truth of the path.

Now I explain it briefly. Birth and death and affliction are the cause and effect of sentient beings; bodhi and nirvāṇa are the cause and effect of all Buddhas. Yet sentient beings and the Buddhas are only names. Birth and death, affliction, bodhi, and nirvāṇa are likewise only names. Speaking ultimately, they are just the one mind. Because from beginningless time one has been deluded about this one mind, all of bodhi and nirvāṇa have become affliction and birth and death. Therefore now, awakening to this one mind, one takes affliction and birth and death as bodhi and nirvāṇa. Though the names are two, the essence is not two. As water becomes ice, and ice returns to water. This is the non-doing four noble truths.

Question: That sentient beings and the Buddhas are only names is indeed so. But birth and death and affliction are defiled dharmas, while bodhi and nirvāṇa are pure dharmas; their rising and sinking are utterly different, their excellence and inferiority as far apart as heaven and earth — how can one say these too are only names? Answer: If one speaks from the standpoint of phenomena, it is as you say; if one speaks from the standpoint of principle, each and every one has no real dharma. It is like an actor in a troupe playing a poor child — his body goes about begging for food, his mind gives rise to yearning; in a moment he plays an emperor — his body mounts the throne, his mind gives rise to joy. A person of wisdom should not, regarding this, give rise to real thoughts, thinking there is a difference of noble and base, high and low. Birth and death and affliction, bodhi and nirvāṇa, are likewise so. Ordinary people take them as real; the Buddhas and sages know them not to be true.

Again it is asked: that birth and death and affliction are not real is acceptable; but if bodhi and nirvāṇa also are not truly real, why must one toil at cultivating and realizing them? Answer: What is said to be "not true" merely destroys attachment; it does not say that cultivation and realization are nonexistent. If one grasps at their not being true, one instead falls into a wrong view. There are those who break the precepts and rules with their bodies while their mouths speak of the profound and subtle, taking Buddha-recitation as the work of fools and cultivation as attachment to marks — this is a great disease of those of the final age who practice Chan with clever minds, and one must know it.

Here, "to be far from evil dharmas, vowing never to create them again" is "the afflictions are inexhaustible, I vow to sever them," the resolve made relying on the truth of accumulation. "To diligently cultivate the sage path, vowing never to be idle and regress" is "the Dharma-gates are measureless, I vow to learn them," the resolve made relying on the truth of the path. "Vowing to attain right enlightenment" is "the Buddha path is supreme, I vow to accomplish it," the resolve made relying on the truth of cessation. "Vowing to deliver sentient beings" is "sentient beings are boundless, I vow to save them," the resolve made relying on the truth of suffering. Though the words are not in sequence (the order of the words is different), the meaning is not two (the meaning is entirely the same).

What is meant by making the resolve relying on the truth of suffering? It means contemplating sentient beings as oppressed by birth, aging, sickness, and death, giving rise to great suffering and distress; because of this cause, one makes the vow: "I shall soon escape birth and death, and also deliver measureless sentient beings so that they escape birth and death." Birth and death are the truth of suffering that is contemplated; because one contemplates birth and death, one vows to deliver them — this is called making the resolve relying on the truth of suffering.

What is meant by making the resolve relying on the truth of accumulation? It means contemplating sentient beings as harmed and distressed by greed, anger, foolishness, and wrong views, unable to extricate themselves; because of this cause, one makes the vow: "I shall sever the afflictions of myself and also sever the measureless afflictions of sentient beings, causing them to attain liberation." Affliction is the truth of accumulation that is contemplated; because one contemplates the harm of affliction, one wishes to cut it off — this is called making the resolve relying on the truth of accumulation.

What is meant by making the resolve relying on the truth of cessation? It means contemplating that the Buddhas have already extinguished affliction, attaining the joy of liberation and possessing measureless spiritual powers and freedom; while sentient beings, unaware and unknowing, falsely undergo all suffering. Because of this cause, one makes the vow: "I shall diligently cultivate skillful means, attaining the joy of the great nirvāṇa's stillness and also causing sentient beings to attain this same joy." Nirvāṇa, the Buddha-fruit, is the truth of cessation that is contemplated; because one contemplates the Buddha-fruit, there is aspiration — this is called making the resolve relying on the truth of cessation.

What is meant by making the resolve relying on the truth of the path? It means contemplating the six perfections, the ten thousand practices, and the Dharma-gates numerous as the sands of the Ganges as possessing measureless Dharma-joy that accords with the nature; while sentient beings do not study or cultivate them, falsely creating all karma. Because of this cause, one makes the vow: "I shall diligently study and cultivate the measureless Dharma-gates and also cause sentient beings to study and cultivate this Dharma." The Dharma-gate is the truth of the path that is contemplated; because one contemplates the Dharma-gate, one vows to study and cultivate — this is called making the resolve relying on the truth of the path.

Yet these are merely phenomenal marks. If one knows that the nature is complete with principle, then all four are non-doing. What is non-doing? It is: sentient beings are provisional names, so there is nothing to save; afflictions have no real nature, so there is nothing to sever; the Dharma-gates are originally complete, so there is nothing to learn; the Buddha path is originally present, so there is nothing to accomplish. This is called the non-doing four great vows, made relying on the non-doing four noble truths."

[The four great vows] also called the "four vast vows." The Buddhas have general vows and particular vows; the four vast vows are the general vow, and every Bodhisattva, when first arousing the resolve, must make this vow. Because the vows are broad and universal, they are called "vast"; because they restrain one's own mind, they are called "vows"; because one's will seeks their fulfillment, they are called "prayers." Relying on the four true truths, these four vows are made. The Essentials of Calm and Contemplation says: first, "sentient beings are boundless, I vow to save them" is the vow, relying on the truth of suffering, to save boundless sentient beings. Second, "the afflictions are measureless, I vow to sever them" is the vow, relying on the truth of accumulation, to sever the endless afflictions. Third, "the Dharma-gates are endless, I vow to learn them" is the vow, relying on the truth of the path, to learn the endless Dharma-gates. Fourth, "the Buddha path is supreme, I vow to accomplish it" is the vow, relying on the truth of cessation, to accomplish the endless Buddha path. The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind says: "All Bodhisattvas also have four vows to accomplish and sustain living beings and to uphold the Three Jewels, never retreating even when the kalpa of the great ocean comes to an end. What are the four? First, vowing to save all sentient beings; second, vowing to sever all afflictions; third, vowing to learn all Dharma-gates; and fourth, vowing to realize all Buddha-fruits."

[The four noble truths] the truth of suffering, the truth of accumulation, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path. First, "the truth of suffering" is the truth that explains the many sufferings of human life. Suffering has the mark of oppressive pressure. Life has the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, and immeasurable other sufferings; suffering is the reality of this present life. Second, "accumulation" in "the truth of accumulation" carries the sense of bringing about and creating, and explains how the suffering of life arises. The suffering of life arises because, through craving, one creates karma and so undergoes suffering and the turning of samsara. Third, "the truth of cessation" is the truth that explains the stilling of all suffering. When all the accumulation of suffering (craving) is forever extinguished without remainder, without defilement and without attachment, one no longer undergoes suffering or samsara — this is the truth of cessation. Fourth, "the truth of the path" explains how to forever sever the accumulation of suffering (craving), that is, the path of stilling suffering. Among the four truths, accumulation is the cause and suffering the effect; the path is the cause and cessation the effect. [The perfect teaching] the supreme and complete doctrine of the Great Vehicle, the fourth of the four teachings established by Tiantai (the Tripitaka teaching, the common teaching, the distinct teaching, and the perfect teaching). [The non-doing four noble truths] established by the Tiantai master Zhiyi, belonging to the exposition of the perfect teaching. It maintains that delusion and awakening are in themselves the reality-mark; the great-vehicle Bodhisattva contemplates all dharmas perfectly, thing after thing being identical with principle, without any contrivance. The non-doing four noble truths are: first, the truth of suffering — contemplating that the five aggregates, the twelve entrances, and so on are all identical with true suchness, having in reality no mark of suffering to be abandoned; second, the truth of accumulation — contemplating that all afflictions and karmic defilements are originally pure by nature, having in reality no mark of accumulating birth and death to be cut off; third, the truth of cessation — contemplating that birth and death and nirvāṇa are originally not two, having in reality no suffering of birth and death to sever and no nirvāṇic stillness to realize; fourth, the truth of the path — contemplating that all dharmas are identical with the middle way, removed from the extreme and wrong views, having no affliction-delusion to sever and no bodhi-path to cultivate. [The reality-mark] what is called "the reality-mark" is the true condition; "the reality-mark of all dharmas" is the true condition of all dharmas. In the Buddha-Treasury Sutra

Chapter Two on Buddha-Recitation, the Buddha says: "What is called the reality-mark of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, having nothing." The Diamond Sutra says: "All formed marks are all false and unreal." [The five aggregates] the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness — the five great elements constituting the human body. [The twelve entrances] the six faculties and the six objects. [The nine-five] refers to the position of a monarch. "Nine-five" is a name of a line position in the Book of Changes, which says: "Nine-five: the flying dragon in the heavens; favorable to see the great man." Hence afterward it is used to refer to the imperial position.

blocks.text: 4. Seeking Rebirth in the Pure Land

inline.s: The Chan contemplation refers to the sixteen contemplations, beginning with the contemplation of the sun, up to the rebirth of the nine grades. One may practice all sixteen contemplations, or single-mindedly one contemplation. As for "a single contemplation," it refers in particular to the comprehensive contemplation, in which one contemplates one's own body seated within a lotus blossom and forms the thought of the lotus opening and closing; when the lotus opens, Amitābha and the holy multitude all release great light, coming to illumine one's body, and the water, birds, and trees all proclaim the wonderful Dharma — this is called the comprehensive contemplation. Or one may simply contemplate the sixteen-foot Buddha-form upon the pond water, with hand lowered in welcome, while one's own body kneels within the blossom — this too may be done. Question: Now that one is single-mindedly holding the Name, why also cause one to contemplate? Answer: Reciting the Name all day, and contemplating for a while — using contemplation to aid the recitation, then the recitation is not scattered. Even if the mind be coarse and the realm subtle, one can rely upon the image to contemplate — what hindrance is there? The Chan contemplation belongs to the waking state; dreams belong to the sleeping. Whether waking or sleeping, one can see the Buddha. If one does not contemplate, then seeing the Buddha is difficult. Question: In contemplation seeing the Buddha — is there not a demonic matter? Answer: A Chan practitioner who originally does not recite the Buddha but has the Buddha suddenly appear — this is the mind and the realm being at odds, and is called a demonic matter. A reciter of the Buddha, who originally contemplates the Buddha, with the Buddha appearing in accordance with the marks — this is called the path of mutual resonance between the mind and the Buddha, not a demonic matter. Yet one must understand that the Buddha seen is like the moon in water, neither existing nor nonexistent, and cannot be grasped; if one gives rise to grasping, one fears it may instead become a demonic matter — be carefully mindful of this. The golden body is the proper retribution; the land adorned with precious treasures is the circumstantial retribution. "Passing through" means experiencing; "adorned with precious treasures" means adorned with the seven treasures."

Because of the anointing with sweet dew, the obstructions of past lives are removed; because the light illumines the body, the roots of goodness grow; because the hand strokes my head, affliction and ignorance are at once broken; because the robe covers my body, the wonderful mind and the true realm appear before me.

Past obstructions' refers to the three obstructions of delusion, karma, and suffering. "Roots of goodness" means the roots of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. The dharmas that cloud and disturb the mind are called "affliction," referring to the delusions of views and thoughts. Not understanding the first, ultimate truth is called "ignorance," referring to the fundamental delusion. Because of these two delusions, the wonderful mind and the true realm cannot appear. Now these two delusions are at once emptied, and so the opening of understanding appears. Perfect enlightenment is the realizing wisdom; the still light is the realized principle. "Appearing before one" means clearly understood and luminous."

At that time, riding upon the diamond dais and following behind the Buddha, within the snapping of a finger I was born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, within a superior lotus blossom in the pool of seven treasures. The lotus at once opened, and I saw Amitābha Buddha and all the great Bodhisattvas, heard the subtle and wondrous sound of Dharma, and upon hearing, realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.

[Diamond dais] This is the throne of one born in the highest grade. The Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life says: When one born in the highest grade is reborn in that land (the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss), "because this person is vigorous and brave, Amitābha Tathāgata, together with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, countless transformation Buddhas, hundreds and thousands of monks and the great assemblies of śrāvakas, immeasurable devas, and palaces of seven treasures — with Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva holding the diamond dais and, together with Mahāsthāmaprāpta, coming before the practitioner — Amitābha Buddha releases a great radiant light, illumining the practitioner's body, and, with all the Bodhisattvas, extends a hand in welcome." [Within a finger-snap] describes an extremely brief time: within a finger-snap.
[Superior lotus blossom] the lotus (flower) within which there is the diamond dais.

[Patience of non-arising] that is the patience of non-arising dharmas, in which true wisdom abides in the principle that "all dharmas originally never arose, and so also never cease," and never again falls back. The Buddha says: "All dharmas are all false and unreal." (Great Parinirvāṇa Sutra, Volume Forty

the Kaundinya Chapter.) All dharmas originally neither arise, and so also do not cease. Yet sentient beings invert true and false, falsely seeing arising and ceasing. Now upon hearing the subtle, wondrous sound of Dharma, one at once opens wisdom and understands that dharmas originally have no arising or ceasing — hence it is said one "attains the patience of non-arising." Having obtained the patience of non-arising, one is a great being of the Dharma-body, endowed with vast spiritual powers and wondrous functions.

[Without departing from the Land of Peace and Nurture] the self-nature does not depart from the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. "Land of Peace and Nurture" is another name for the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life says: "The Buddhas tell the Bodhisattvas to go visit the Buddha of the Land of Peace and Nurture." [Ground of non-retrogression] the stage of non-retrogression, transliterated "Avivartika." This means that having been born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss one only advances to Buddhahood and never regresses. [Land] transliterated "kṣetra," translated as "field," "land," "country," "place" — that is, the land of a Buddha; combining Sanskrit and Chinese, "buddha-field." "Buddha-field" means the land of a Buddha.

Question: The Bodhisattva transforms others not in the Pure Land but in the defiled land — why? Answer: Because in the Pure Land people have goodness and no evil, so transforming and delivering them is easy; in the defiled land there is much evil and little goodness, so transforming and delivering them is difficult. Because it is difficult, great compassion grows and the practice of the vow becomes firm; because it is easy, the mind of compassion is not deep and the practice of the vow is not broad. The Larger Amitābha Sutra says "one day of cultivation in this world surpasses one kalpa of cultivation in the Western Pure Land" — it is precisely on account of this. Moreover, this Saha world is the place where one was born in the past; the connections must surely be many, and the transforming of them is urgent. Therefore, having been born in the Pure Land, one must first return here. Question: Why not simply transform and guide sentient beings right here in this world — what is wrong with that? Why must one leave this and go there, and only then return? Answer: If one does not leave this world, then one is liable to fall; where could transforming and guiding begin? If one does not go there, then self-benefit is not yet accomplished; how could one secure benefiting others? It is like a poor man who has not yet seen the emperor nor received office — he himself is too busy with hunger, cold, and want to provide for his neighbors and townsfolk. Hence one knows: if one is unwilling to deliver sentient beings, that is that; if one is willing, then one must seek the West. If one is not born in the West, that is that; having been born there, one must return. Question: Just now one wished to be reborn there, and now wishes to return — is this not a hesitant advance and retreat, an undecided will? Answer: The earlier stage seeks self-benefit, therefore one vows to be reborn there; the later stage wishes to benefit others, therefore one must return. Though the resolve is made at one time, the action has a sequence. If one did not first make this intention, then once born in the Pure Land, returning would be difficult — what then of the four kinds of kindness and the three realms? Hence one knows: before attaining rebirth, one is resolved never to beget the thought of again entering the womb; having been born in the Land of Peace and Nurture, one is resolved never to lack the mind of coming back to transform and guide. This precisely shows the certainty. How can one call it undecided? (Therefore, before one has been reborn, one has already resolved never again to give rise to the thought of entering the womb; and being born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one is resolved never to lack the mind of returning to the Saha world to transform and guide sentient beings. This is precisely the certainty of the intention; how can one call it undecided?)

Question: In the West one does not regress; but if one returns to the Saha world, is there still regression? Answer: As made clear above, the three bodies and four wisdoms and the rest appear in full, and moreover with Amitābha's protective mindfulness and the Buddhas' sustaining, how can there be any principle of regression! It is like returning to one's home village wearing brocade, plying the oars with a following wind — no seeking that is not advantageous, no going that does not advance. The Bodhisattva's delivering of sentient beings is necessarily preceded by seeking rebirth in the West before returning — indeed for this reason."

Master Xing'an's Commentary on the Western Pure Land Text says: "Such great vows — this sums up the preceding text. 'Worlds inexhaustible' and the rest are examples used to state, in summary, that my vow is inexhaustible. As when it is said: the worlds cannot be exhausted, therefore my vow cannot be exhausted; sentient beings cannot be exhausted, karma and afflictions cannot be exhausted, therefore my vow cannot be exhausted; if these four could be exhausted, then my vow could be exhausted. Question: Why set forth this inexhaustible vow? Answer: Because mind is inexhaustible; the vows one makes in accordance with the mind are likewise without end. Moreover, 'worlds...' and the other four all exist within the mind; even upon becoming a Buddha, there is no principle by which they could be exhausted. Question: Since the vow is inexhaustible, when will one become a Buddha? Answer: What is called 'becoming a Buddha' is only recognizing that one's own mind in the end does not arise. As for the thirty-two marks, which are skillfully displayed as a matter of convenience — they are in themselves not real; what is there to discuss of accomplishment and non-accomplishment?"
